intro: Trieste holds Italy's densest cluster of registered monumental trees, 48 by the city's own count. Twelve stand within three hundred metres of each other in the park an archduke planted on a limestone headland, testing conifers from California. Twelve more, mostly London planes, grow in a public garden a botanist mayor planted in 1854. Four, two bagolari and two elms, stand across the old city and San Giusto. The rest stand alone or in pairs: pines, a sinkhole oak, a chestnut at Opicina, a maple and lime at Basovizza, a university oak, a plane on the road to Miramare.
meta_description: Thirty-six remarkable trees in Trieste: Maximilian's Californian conifers, a botanist mayor's planes, and a karst sinkhole oak.
question_meta: The oldest tree in Trieste is the London plane at the Boschetto roundabout on Viale al Cacciatore, over 200 years old and older than any park in the city.
question_answer: The oldest tree in Trieste is the London plane standing at the Boschetto roundabout on Viale al Cacciatore, which the municipality puts at over 200 years. That makes it older than every public garden in the city, including the Giardino Pubblico laid out in 1854 and the park at Miramare begun in 1856. It is five metres round the trunk and twenty-five metres tall. The largest tree in Trieste is a different plane, in the Giardino Pubblico, at 542 centimetres of girth and about 180 years old.
question_context: Nothing in Italy's official record of monumental trees will tell you a tree's age. The national MASAF register lists 47 protected trees in the comune of Trieste with species, girth, height and a coordinate, and the regional Friuli Venezia Giulia decree that feeds it adds a place name and the legal reason for each designation, but neither carries an age field or any note of whether a tree is still healthy. Every date on this page therefore comes from elsewhere: from the municipality's own survey of its 48 oldest trees, which puts the Viale al Cacciatore plane above 200 years and the great plane of the Giardino Pubblico near 180, and from the founding dates of the gardens themselves. Those dates are firm. Muzio de Tommasini, botanist and podesta, began the public garden in 1854 on land bought from Benedictine nuns and planted the planes himself. Archduke Maximilian of Habsburg started the Miramare park in the spring of 1856 and kept ordering plants for it even after he had left for Mexico. A tree in either place is as old as the garden around it or a little younger, which is the honest way to date most of this list.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Trieste?
faq.a: The London plane at the Boschetto roundabout on Viale al Cacciatore, which the city puts at over 200 years. It is older than the Giardino Pubblico and older than the Miramare park, both of which were planted in the 1850s.

In eight walks, not one. Twelve trees stand inside three hundred metres of each other in the Miramare park, eight kilometres up the coast: the castle's conifers, a holm oak and six Aleppo pines share the same paths. Twelve more, mostly London planes, cluster around the Giardino Pubblico off Via Giulia, the garden its own 1854 founder planted. A hackberry in Piazza Hortis, an elm in the Piazzale Rosmini garden, a second elm at the Civico Museo Sartorio and a second hackberry up on the cathedral hill of San Giusto stand across Citta Vecchia, San Vito and San Giusto. Two Aleppo pines share the hillside park at Villa Revoltella. A Turkey oak stands alone over a sinkhole in the Percedol nature reserve on the karst plateau. A horse chestnut stands alone at Opicina, a tram ride from the centre. A maple and a lime, a few hundred metres apart, stand in and beside the village of Basovizza near the Slovenian border. And two more stand alone: a downy oak on the university campus, and a plane on the road up to Miramare.

faq.q: Do they cost anything to see?
faq.a: No. The Miramare park is free and open daily, and the castle inside it is the only part you pay for. The Giardino Pubblico is a free public park and the Boschetto plane stands on a public street.

faq.q: Why are there Californian trees at Miramare?
faq.a: Because Maximilian treated the park as an experiment. He wanted to know which foreign species would survive on bare Adriatic limestone, and within ten years the garden had cedars from Lebanon, North Africa and the Himalaya, cypresses from California and Mexico, and the redwoods that are still the tallest things in it.

faq.q: What is the Foiba di Basovizza?
faq.a: Italy's National Monument to the victims of the foibe, a disused mine shaft used in May 1945 for the execution of Italian civilians and soldiers by occupying Yugoslav troops, and the principal memorial for families of the deported. The grounds are free and open every day. A Montpellier maple that was already over a century old that spring still grows on the site.

trees.name: The Redwood of Miramare

location.address: Parco del Castello di Miramare, Viale Miramare, 34151 Trieste

trees.story: The man who planted this tree was shot by a firing squad in Mexico eleven years later. Archduke Maximilian of Habsburg began the Miramare park in the spring of 1856 on a limestone headland with almost no soil on it, and he treated the whole thing as an experiment: he wanted to find out which foreign species would hold on to bare Adriatic rock. Soil was carted in. Within ten years the garden had cedars from Lebanon, North Africa and the Himalaya, firs from Spain, cypresses from California and Mexico, and this coast redwood from the fog belt of northern California. Maximilian kept ordering plants for it after he sailed for Mexico to be crowned emperor, and he never came back. The redwood took. It is now 4.25 metres round the trunk and thirty metres tall, the largest of the two redwoods here and one of twelve protected trees standing within three hundred metres of each other. Put a hand on it. The bark is soft, dry and fibrous rather than hard, and on old trees it goes thirty centimetres deep, which is what lets a redwood walk out of a fire that kills everything around it. This one is a child by the standards of its species, which passes 115 metres at home.

trees.name: The Monterey Cypress of Miramare

location.address: Parco del Castello di Miramare, Viale Miramare, 34151 Trieste

trees.story: In the wild this species survives in two groves on the California coast, together covering less than a square kilometre, and it is listed as threatened. Planted anywhere else with sea air, it grows into one of the fastest and heaviest conifers a garden can hold. That is the paradox of the Monterey cypress, and this is what it looks like when it goes well: 4.1 metres round the trunk, eighteen metres tall, and far wider than it is high, because an old Monterey cypress stops climbing and starts spreading until the crown flattens out like a table. Maximilian's gardeners put it in after 1856 among the cypresses ordered from California and Mexico, and on a headland that gets the bora full in the face it has done the thing the archduke was testing for. The wind has pushed the whole crown away from the sea, so the tree leans its weight inland and reads as a permanent record of the direction the worst weather comes from. Crush a leaf between your fingers and it smells of lemon. The Italian sources describing the park call this simply the cypress, and one of them names the wrong species for it, so trust the trunk rather than the label.

trees.name: The Ghost Pine of Miramare

location.address: Parco del Castello di Miramare, Viale Miramare, 34151 Trieste

trees.story: Trieste calls this one il pino fantasma, the ghost pine, and the name is a description rather than a flourish. Its needles are long, grey and set so thinly on the branch that you can see straight through the crown to the sky behind it, which no other pine in the park lets you do. Stand under it on a bright day and the tree casts almost no shadow. It comes from the dry foothills that ring California's Central Valley, where it grows on serpentine and rubble that defeats everything else, and it was one of the more eccentric things Maximilian's gardeners were given to try. Italy's register protects it on grounds of botanical rarity, a category only two trees in the whole Trieste list are given. The cones are the other reason to come. A ghost pine cone is the size of a human head, weighs up to a kilogram, and hangs on hooked scales that will draw blood if you grab one wrongly; the people who lived in its native range ate the seeds, which are large and oily and worth the trouble. At 2.5 metres round and twenty metres tall it is not the biggest tree here, and it is the strangest.

trees.name: The Greek Strawberry Tree of Miramare

location.address: Parco del Castello di Miramare, Viale Miramare, 34151 Trieste

trees.story: This is a shrub that forgot to stop. Arbutus andrachne normally tops out as a thick bush on a Greek or Turkish hillside, and the Italian register lists this one at 2.04 metres round the trunk and twelve metres tall, which for the species is close to absurd. It is the reason the tree is protected on botanical rarity as well as on size. The bark is the thing to look at. Each summer the outer layer peels away in thin sheets like sunburn, and what is left underneath is a bare trunk the colour of cinnamon, cool and slightly waxy to touch, with no fissures anywhere on it. Run a hand along it and the surface feels closer to skin than to timber. Maximilian's gardeners planted it after 1856 among the Mediterranean species that were meant to prove the headland could hold a garden, and unlike the common strawberry tree it was never a safe bet this far north. Fifty-nine of its common cousins, Arbutus unedo, grow a couple of hundred metres away as a registered stand, and none of them has done what this one did. Its flowers come as small white bells in spring, its fruit as round orange berries.

trees.name: The Great Plane of the Giardino Pubblico

location.address: Giardino Pubblico Muzio de Tommasini, Via Giulia, 34126 Trieste

trees.story: The city dug up the pavement around this tree and threw it away. The Giardino Pubblico's biggest plane is 542 centimetres round the trunk and thirty-four metres tall, the largest tree in Trieste by measurement, and the paving laid over its root plate was slowly suffocating it, so the municipality broke the surface out and replaced it with draining material. That is what caring for a 180 year old tree in a city actually looks like. The garden around it was begun in 1854 by Muzio de Tommasini, a serious botanist who happened also to be the podesta of Trieste, on ground bought from Benedictine nuns after a plan to build a church and housing there was dropped. He planted the planes himself. Three hectares now hold roughly 320 large trees from five continents, arranged along paths lined with the bronze heads of Triestine writers, and Italo Svevo walked here often enough that the garden turns up in what he wrote. Nine planes in this garden are on Italy's monumental register and this is the heaviest of them. Stand back far enough to take in the whole trunk: the bark flakes off in plates and leaves the pale patchwork that is the only thing about a London plane you can identify from a hundred metres.

trees.name: The Twin Horse Chestnuts of the Giardino Pubblico
trees.age_estimate: about 170 years, planted with the garden from 1854

location.address: Giardino Pubblico Muzio de Tommasini, Via Giulia, 34126 Trieste

trees.story: Two horse chestnuts stand thirty metres apart in this garden and the register measured both at exactly 335 centimetres of girth and exactly twenty-three metres of height. Identical to the centimetre, listed as two separate protected trees, and there is no way to tell from the paper which is which. They were almost certainly planted together when Muzio de Tommasini laid the garden out from 1854, and they have grown at the same rate for 170 years because nothing has happened to one that did not happen to the other. A third, slightly smaller at 317 centimetres, stands further north. Come in May. The horse chestnut is one of the few big trees that flowers in a way you notice from the other end of a park, holding hundreds of white candles upright on the ends of the branches, each one flecked with yellow that turns pink once the flower has been visited and no longer wants bees. The species itself is not from anywhere near here. It was unknown to western Europe until the sixteenth century and comes from a handful of mountain valleys in Albania and Greece, where it is now endangered in the wild.

trees.name: The Valonia Oak of the Giardino Pubblico
trees.age_estimate: about 170 years, planted with the garden from 1854

location.address: Giardino Pubblico Muzio de Tommasini, Via Giulia, 34126 Trieste

trees.story: This is the only valonia oak in Friuli Venezia Giulia, and it is the only tree on Trieste's entire monumental register protected for botanical rarity and nothing else. Every other entry earns its place on size, age or the look of the thing. This one is here because there is no second example within a region of 1.2 million people. At 179 centimetres round it is also one of the smallest trees on the list, which tells you how little the measurement matters in this case. The acorns are the reason the species was ever worth anything. A valonia acorn sits in a cup covered in thick shaggy scales that curl outward like a sea anemone, and those cups are extraordinarily rich in tannin. For centuries the eastern Mediterranean shipped them west by the boatload to tan leather, and the trade was large enough that the Greek and Turkish groves were managed for it. The species is semi-evergreen, holding tired leaves through mild winters and dropping them late. It grows wild in Greece, western Turkey and one wood in Puglia. Muzio de Tommasini, a botanist before he was a mayor, would have known exactly how unusual it was to put one in the ground here.

trees.name: The Plane of the Boschetto Roundabout

location.address: Viale al Cacciatore, rotonda del Boschetto, 34142 Trieste

trees.story: Trieste's oldest tree stands on a traffic roundabout. The municipality's survey of its 48 monumental trees puts this London plane above 200 years, which makes it older than every park in the city: older than the Giardino Pubblico begun in 1854 a kilometre downhill, older than the Miramare park begun in 1856, older than the Ferdinandeo villa on the slope above it. It was in the ground when Trieste was still Austria's only real seaport and the road it stands on was a country lane. It is five metres and ten centimetres round the trunk and twenty-five metres tall. The London plane was the tree of choice for the avenues and gardens Trieste built in the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries, which is why nearly a fifth of the city's protected trees are planes, and this is the survivor from the first of those plantings. A second registered plane stands twenty-five metres away, 440 centimetres round, and the two of them frame the entrance to the Boschetto del Ferdinandeo, the wooded hill that Triestini have walked up on Sunday afternoons for as long as the trees have been there. Take Via Giulia out of the public garden and keep climbing.

trees.name: The Bagolaro of Piazza Hortis

location.address: Piazza Attilio Hortis, 34123 Trieste

trees.story:
For over 180 years this hackberry has stood in what is now Piazza Hortis, and for most of that time nobody thought about what people were doing to its roots. In 2025 the city fenced it off: pedestrians had been crossing the square for generations without knowing they were walking on top of nearly two centuries of root plate, compacting the soil the tree breathes through. The comune spent about 17,000 euros on the fence and on new drainage-friendly planting around the base, part of a wider programme that has already stripped suffocating pavement away from monumental trees elsewhere in the city.

Trieste has identified 48 monumental trees within its borders, the highest concentration the comune has recorded of any Italian city, and this bagolaro is one of them. In September 2024 it was fitted with a TreeTag, a small ID marker placed as part of a European citizen-science campaign that measures a tree's condition and records the data for researchers to track over time.

Celtis australis is native across the Mediterranean and famously slow to give up: its wood was used for cart axles and ploughshares because it resists splitting even when green. This one has outlived the square's own name twice over, and the piazza, library and street around it are all named for Attilio Hortis, the Trieste historian and librarian who died a century ago.

trees.name: The Siberian Elm of Piazzale Rosmini

location.address: Giardino di Piazzale Antonio Rosmini, 34123 Trieste

trees.story:
The garden at Piazzale Rosmini climbs the San Vito hill above the church of Madonna del Mare, nine and a half thousand square metres of slope and lawn that the city's own parks department singles out for two things: its valuable trees and its play areas for children of different ages. The Siberian elm growing there, 3.58 metres round and 24 metres tall, is one of Trieste's registered monumental specimens and the garden's standout tree.

Ulmus pumila earned its place in European gardens for the same reason it earns a mention here: it shrugs off Dutch elm disease far better than the native field and wych elms the fungus devastated across the continent from the 1970s onward. A healthy elm of real size in a European city is worth noticing partly for that reason alone, a survivor by constitution rather than by luck.

Like the bagolaro at Piazza Hortis, this elm was fitted with a TreeTag in September 2024, part of the same citywide EU citizen-science campaign that is slowly building a public record of condition and growth for Trieste's 48 monumental trees. No individual age has been published for it, so none is claimed here.

trees.story:
The park came with a condition attached to it. Pasquale Revoltella left his grounds above Via Fabio Severo to the city of Trieste on the terms that they stay free and stay open, and five hectares of hillside are still a municipal garden that charges nobody anything and unlocks its gates at seven in the morning. A national parks and gardens competition later voted it the most beautiful park in Italy.

Two Aleppo pines inside it hold Italy's monumental-tree protection, standing about fifty metres apart. This is the thicker of the pair and the shorter, 360 centimetres round the trunk and eighteen metres tall, where its neighbour is slimmer and carries four metres more height. Pinus halepensis is the pine of the dry Mediterranean, the species that takes bare limestone where nothing else will hold on, and the karst Trieste sits on is exactly that ground. Its cones are small, hard and slow, sitting closed on the branch for years at a time.

Nobody has put a number of years on either tree. The regional register measured this one in 2025 and left the age column empty, Il Piccolo photographed a monumental Aleppo pine here in 2018 without dating it, and girth on its own will not settle the question for this species in this climate. If you know of a figure with a real basis behind it, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, 3.6 metres round, thicker than its neighbour and four metres shorter. It stands about fifty metres north of the park's other protected Aleppo pine, well inside the grounds.

trees.story:
Trieste keeps a plan for the day its biggest trees come down. Seventy-eight of them were surveyed one at a time for the risk of failure, and this pine is on that list, entered as a trunk 110 centimetres across in the park at Villa Revoltella. Convert it and you get 346 centimetres round, which is what the regional register measured here, and fourteen centimetres less than the other protected Aleppo pine standing fifty metres away. Two pines, two sets of figures. That arithmetic is the only thing proving this hillside holds a pair rather than one tree counted twice.

This is the taller of them by four metres, twenty-two to the top, and the slimmer. Pinus halepensis does not grow to order: it leans, forks low and carries its needles in loose tufts at the ends of long bare limbs, so an old one reads as an open, see-through tree rather than a column, and a slope exaggerates the habit further. The register protected it on size and on the character of the stand it belongs to.

What the register gave no answer to is how old it is, and neither does anything else published about this park. A dated planting record for the Revoltella grounds would settle both pines at once, and somebody in Trieste may well have one.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by being the taller and slimmer of the two, twenty-two metres up and 3.46 metres round. It stands about fifty metres south of the park's thicker, shorter Aleppo pine.

location.address: Giardino del Civico Museo Sartorio, Largo Papa Giovanni XXIII 1, 34123 Trieste

https://www.ilpiccolo.it/cronaca/quindici-pini-olmi-e-platani-nel-gruppo-degli-alberi-vip-jm8b46dd (names 'l'olmo del Caucaso di Villa Sartorio' as one of four monumental trees owned by the Comune di Trieste)

https://www.triesteprima.it/social/giardini-storici-trieste-villa-sartorio-2019.html (gives the same tree at 111cm trunk diameter, about 349cm circumference, and 22m height, consistent with the register figures)
https://museosartoriotrieste.it/civico-museo-sartorio/ (Museo Sartorio opening hours and free admission)
trees.access: Free. The tree stands in the garden of the Civico Museo Sartorio, a municipal museum with free admission, open Monday to Friday 9:00-18:00 and Saturday 9:00-13:00
trees.transport: About a 12-15 min walk south-west of Piazza Unita d'Italia, near Piazza Hortis
trees.story:
Italy's monumental-tree register holds this elm twice. One sheet calls it the tree of Villa Sartorio on Via dei Modiano and gives 353 centimetres of girth and 23 metres of height; another calls it the tree of the Giardino Sartorio and gives 350 and 20. The two records sit forty-three metres apart, which is the width of a garden rather than the distance between two trees, and every independent account of the place, the newspaper's, the museum's and the city's, describes exactly one Caucasian elm here. One tree, two files. It is also why the pin on this page is marked approximate: nobody can say which of the two readings lands closer to the trunk.

The Comune di Trieste owns only four monumental trees outright, and this is one of them. In 2026 all four went into a municipal programme of roughly 135,000 euros for survey and selective pruning, this elm alongside the two great planes of the Giardino Pubblico.

Zelkova carpinifolia comes from the Caucasus and the Caspian forests of northern Iran and reached European gardens in the eighteenth century. It is not a true elm, whatever the name says. Its leaves are small and evenly toothed, nearer a hornbeam's than an elm's, which is exactly what carpinifolia means. Nobody has published an age for it, so we offer none; if you know when it went into this garden, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the leaves, small and evenly toothed like a hornbeam's, on the only Caucasian elm in the garden. It stands behind the Civico Museo Sartorio near Piazza Hortis, and the pin is rough, so look for the tree.

best_time.label: October to November: the whole crown turns orange-brown, the tree's best-known moment after its shape

trees.name: The Horse Chestnut of Via Nazionale

location.address: Via Nazionale 51, Opicina, 34151 Trieste

trees.access: Free to view; stands beside the public sidewalk on Via Nazionale (the SR58/E61 state road through Opicina). Caveat: no independent source confirms whether the trunk itself sits behind a private gate at no. 51, only that the frontage is a public street with a footway running past it
trees.transport: Opicina is reached by bus 39/42 or the Trieste-Opicina tram from Piazza Oberdan, then a short walk on Via Nazionale
trees.story:
Trieste's protected trees stand in designed grounds: a Habsburg's experimental headland, the public garden a botanist mayor laid out, the wooded hill above it. This one stands on a state road. The horse chestnut at Via Nazionale 51 grows up on the karst plateau at Opicina, a tram ride out of Piazza Oberdan, with the SR58 running past it and a footway in between.

It is 324 centimetres round and fifteen metres tall, and the honest thing to say next is that we know nothing else about it. Neither of Il Piccolo's surveys of the city's old trees mentions an Opicina chestnut. No age has ever been published. The only document that names it is the protection order itself, issued nationally and republished by the region, which is one source wearing two covers rather than two sources. The frontage is public and has a pavement along it; whether the trunk itself sits just inside a gate at number 51 is the one thing we could not settle from here.

Come in May. A horse chestnut in flower holds hundreds of white spikes upright at once and reads as a flowering tree from the far end of the street. By August most European ones are going brown, from a leaf-mining moth that crossed the continent in the 1990s, and the walk is worth less. If anybody up there knows this tree's age, or owns a tape measure, we would like to hear it.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, 3.24 metres round on a fifteen-metre tree, standing right at the roadside rather than in a park. It stands beside the pavement at Via Nazionale 51, on the state road through Opicina.

best_time.label: May, when the white flower spikes go up all over the crown

trees.name: The Holm Oak of Miramare

location.address: Parco del Castello di Miramare, Viale Miramare, 34151 Trieste

verified_sources: http://decreti.regione.fvg.it/Storage/2025_71/ALLEGATO1%20AL%20DPReg%20071-2025.PDF (FVG regional decree, same sheet, criteria a,b,e,f,g)

https://ilregistrodeglialberi.it/3846-leccio-trieste-ts-friuli-venezia-giulia (RAMI citizen register, same AMI code 02/L424/TS/06, independent field measurement dated 14/10/2021: circumference 5.20 m, height 25.00 m, estimated age 145 years, 'calcolato in base all'anno di nascita registrato' i.e. derived from a registered planting/birth year)
trees.access: Free, the park is open daily. Only the castle charges admission (same as tri_001-004)
trees.transport: Bus 6 from Piazza Oberdan to Grignano, about 25 min, then a short walk into the park
trees.story:
Two official surveys disagree about how many trunks this tree has. The regional decree's sheet records three stems, of 267, 230 and 250 centimetres round. An independent field measurement made in October 2021 for Italy's citizen tree register found a single trunk of 5.20 metres and noted specifically that it is not multi-stemmed. Nobody has been back to settle it, and the height is unsettled too, at 25 metres by one reading and 28 by the other.

What is not in doubt is what it is doing here. Archduke Maximilian of Habsburg began this garden in 1856 on a limestone headland with almost no soil on it, had earth carted in, and filled it with conifers from California, Mexico, the Himalaya and Lebanon. The holm oak is the other kind of tree at Miramare: an evergreen broadleaf of the Mediterranean coast, small dark leaves held hard through the winter, no season in which it drops them. It is one of twelve protected trees standing within three hundred metres of each other.

Its age is given as about 145 years, calculated from a registered planting year rather than from the wood, so take a decade either side. Maximilian sailed for Mexico to be crowned emperor and was shot by a firing squad in 1867. The park went on being planted without him, and this oak is part of what came after.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, about 5.2 metres round, and by small dark leaves it keeps all winter. It stands among the twelve protected trees of Miramare park; the park has other holm oaks, so the girth is what tells it apart.

trees.name: The Aleppo Pine of Miramare

location.address: Parco del Castello di Miramare, Viale Miramare, 34151 Trieste

verified_sources: https://www.masaf.gov.it/flex/cm/pages/ServeBLOB.php/L/IT/IDPagina/11260 (MASAF national monumental-tree register, sheet 22/L424/TS/06, girth 310cm, height 19m)

https://ilregistrodeglialberi.it/3847-pino-daleppo-trieste-ts-friuli-venezia-giulia (RAMI citizen register, same AMI code 22/L424/TS/06, independent field measurement dated 14/10/2021: circumference 3.10 m matching the register, estimated age 130 years 'calcolato in base all'anno di nascita registrato')
trees.access: Free, the park is open daily. Only the castle charges admission (same as tri_001-004)
trees.transport: Bus 6 from Piazza Oberdan to Grignano, about 25 min, then a short walk into the park
trees.story:
Six Aleppo pines in this park carry the same protection, all within three hundred metres of each other, and this is not the largest of them. The biggest measures 3.68 metres round the trunk; this one is 3.10. It is here because it is the only one of the six that anybody has put a date to: about 130 years, calculated by Italy's citizen tree register from a recorded planting year rather than from the wood, so read it as a decade either way.

That would make it a good forty years younger than the garden it stands in. Archduke Maximilian began Miramare in 1856 by carting soil onto bare limestone to find out which foreign species would hold on to Adriatic rock. The Aleppo pine needed no such help. It is the pine of the Mediterranean shoreline, at home on thin stony ground and salt air, with an open crown that lets the light through and cones that can stay shut on the branch for years, waiting for heat to open them.

It is 19 metres tall, and here is the honest part: at this coordinate you will find several trunks of much the same thickness, none of them separately named or described in any register we could find. Nobody has photographed this one closely enough to tell it from its neighbours. If you work out which is which, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, 3.10 metres round under a 19 metre crown. Five other protected Aleppo pines stand within a few hundred metres, the largest of them 3.68 metres round, so a tape is the only thing that separates them.

trees.name: The Bagolaro of San Giusto

location.address: Piazzale della Cattedrale, Colle di San Giusto, 34121 Trieste

verified_sources: https://ilregistrodeglialberi.it/15992-il-bagolaro-di-san-giusto-bagolaro-trieste-ts-friuli-venezia-giulia (RAMI citizen register: circumference 3.77 m measured 28/12/2023, health 'sufficiente' with two large branch amputations noted, no official AMI/MASAF code assigned to this specimen)

https://www.triesteallnews.it/2020/03/lalbero-di-san-giusto-piu-di-centanni-fa-una-domenica-di-primavera/ (TRIESTE.news/triesteallnews.it: the tree was planted 29 March 1914 in a public ceremony, a procession of hundreds of students from the Ginnastica Triestina society carried it up to San Giusto, planted in the presence of vice-mayor engineer Costantino Doria; poet Riccardo Pitteri wrote 'Per l'albero di San Giusto' for the occasion)

https://www.ilpiccolo.it/cronaca/alberi-monumentali-di-trieste-enrico-8220-ricky8221-ramazzina-presenta-il-bagolaro-di-san-giusto-wbo68nfc (Il Piccolo, part of a civic project where named citizens 'present'/adopt one of the city's monumental trees each; confirms the tree's identity and location independently of RAMI)
trees.access: Free, standing in the open public square in front of the cathedral, on the San Giusto hill; always accessible (the adjoining castle and museum charge admission separately, the square and cathedral forecourt do not)
trees.transport: About a 15 minute uphill walk from Piazza Unita d'Italia via Via Capitolina/Via della Cattedrale, or bus 24 to San Giusto
trees.story:
Hundreds of schoolchildren carried this tree up the hill. On Sunday 29 March 1914 a procession from the Ginnastica Triestina gymnastic society walked a young hackberry to the top of the San Giusto hill and planted it in the square in front of the cathedral, watched by the vice-mayor, the engineer Costantino Doria. The poet Riccardo Pitteri wrote a piece for the day, Per l'albero di San Giusto. Trieste was then the Austro-Hungarian empire's great seaport. Four months later the empire was at war.

The citizen register that measured it says it replaced a tree felled in 1906 after storm damage, which no other source we found repeats, so treat that as one register's note rather than settled history. What is measured is the trunk: 3.77 metres round on 28 December 2023, with the same survey rating its health as fair rather than good and recording two large branches cut away. That is a reasonable state for a tree standing alone on an open hilltop in a city known for its wind.

Celtis australis is what Italian towns plant where nothing else will hold, a species that takes drought, poor soil and limestone without complaint. This one has the best address in Trieste, on the square between the cathedral of San Giusto and the castle, with the whole gulf below it. It carries no national monument code. That is a gap in the paperwork rather than in the tree.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, 3.77 metres round, and by the two large branches that have been cut from its crown. It stands by itself on the open square in front of the cathedral of San Giusto, between the church and the castle.

trees.name: The Turkey Oak of Dolina Percedol

location.address: Dolina di Percedol nature reserve, Carso plateau, Trieste (near Trebiciano/Gropada)

verified_sources: https://www.masaf.gov.it/flex/cm/pages/ServeBLOB.php/L/IT/IDPagina/11260 (MASAF national monumental-tree register, sheet 04/L424/TS/06, girth 310cm, height 35m)

https://ilregistrodeglialberi.it/3841-cerro-trieste-ts-friuli-venezia-giulia (RAMI citizen register, same AMI code 04/L424/TS/06, independent measurement dated 14/10/2021 confirms circumference 3.10 m and height 35.00 m exactly, altitude 300m a.s.l., own accessibility rating 'Accessibile')

https://www.informatrieste.eu/ts/blog/oasi-naturali-a-trieste-visitare-lo-stagno-di-percedol/ (informatrieste.eu, describes Percedol as an 'Oasi di protezione naturale', a marked path around the dolina lined with Turkey oaks)
https://museostorianaturaletrieste.it/wp-content/uploads/2017/11/4-Percedol.pdf (Trieste natural history museum's own description of the reserve)
trees.access: Free, a marked public path circles the dolina inside a protected natural area (Oasi di protezione naturale di Percedol); no fee or gate reported by any source checked
trees.transport: On the Carso plateau above Trieste near Opicina/Trebiciano; reachable by car or local Carso bus lines from Opicina, roughly 20-30 minutes from the city centre. I have not verified an exact bus number or stop, so treat this as an approximate description rather than a checked route
trees.story:
Trieste used to go skating here. The pond at the bottom of the Percedol dolina, a sinkhole in the limestone of the plateau above the city, lies deep enough in its own shade to hold ice through the winter, and in the 1800s and early 1900s that made it the city's rink. Turkey oaks ring the hollow. This is the one the state wrote down.

Thirty-five metres is a great deal of Quercus cerris. Three separate readings exist, from the national monumental register, the regional decree and an independent field visit in October 2021, and all three came back with the same two numbers: 3.10 metres round the trunk, 35 metres tall. That degree of agreement is rare in this work, and it describes a tall, straight tree rather than a broad one.

Nobody has dated it. Neither register carries an age for this oak, and no growth-rate estimate has been made from the girth, so the honest answer is that we do not know. If you know of a survey that dates the oaks of Percedol, tell us.

The setting carries the walk on its own. A dolina is a hollow where limestone has dissolved away beneath, and this is one of the best known on the Trieste Carso, with a marked path around its rim, a protected pond at the bottom and, in the shade below, what local sources call the finest Turkey oaks on the plateau.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its height, 35 metres on a trunk only 3.10 metres round, which is tall and narrow for a Turkey oak. It stands with the other oaks ringing the Percedol dolina, beside the marked path around the sinkhole.

trees.name: The Maple of the Foiba di Basovizza

location.address: Foiba di Basovizza - Monumento Nazionale, Strada Statale 14, Basovizza, 34016 Trieste

verified_sources: https://www.masaf.gov.it/flex/cm/pages/ServeBLOB.php/L/IT/IDPagina/11260 (MASAF national monumental-tree register, sheet 47/L424/TS/06, girth 256cm, height 13m)

https://ilregistrodeglialberi.it/3839-acero-minore-trieste-ts-friuli-venezia-giulia (RAMI citizen register, same AMI code 47/L424/TS/06, independent field measurement dated 14/10/2021: circumference 2.35 m, height 14.00 m, estimated age approx 205 years 'calcolato in base all'anno di nascita registrato')

https://www.discover-trieste.it/vivi/arte-e-cultura/musei/foiba-di-basovizza-monumento-nazionale (official tourism board page on the memorial: declared National Monument 1992, free entry, always open, reached by bus 51 from Trieste Centrale or bus 39 from Cattinara, about 20 min by car from the station)
trees.access: Free, always open with no restricted hours for the memorial grounds themselves; the on-site documentation centre keeps seasonal hours (10:00-18:00 March-June, 10:00-14:00 July-February, closed Wednesdays in the second period)
trees.transport: Bus 51 from Trieste Centrale station, or bus 39 from Cattinara hospital; about 20 minutes by car from the station
trees.story:
This maple was already well over a century old in May 1945, when the shaft it stands beside was used to kill people. The Foiba di Basovizza is a disused mine pit on the karst above Trieste. In the weeks after the German surrender, occupying Yugoslav troops threw Italian civilians and soldiers into it. Italy declared the site a national monument in 1992, and it is the principal place of mourning for those families and for the Triestines deported to camps in Yugoslavia in the same period. Entry is free and the grounds are open at any hour.

The tree is an Acer monspessulanum, the small three-lobed maple of dry Mediterranean limestone, a species that seldom grows large. This one has reached 13 metres, and its trunk measures either 2.56 metres round or 2.35, depending on which survey you read: the national register recorded the larger figure, an independent field visit in October 2021 the smaller. Its age is given as about 205 years, calculated from a registered birth year rather than from the wood, so read it as two decades either way.

People come to Basovizza for the monument and not for a tree, and that is the right order. The maple is older than any of it, older than the memorial and older than what the memorial records. The documentation centre beside it keeps seasonal hours. The grounds, and the maple, do not close.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the leaves, small and blunt and in three lobes rather than the five most maples carry. It stands on the memorial grounds at the Foiba di Basovizza, 13 metres tall on a trunk about two and a half metres round.

trees.name: The Lime of Basovizza

location.address: Basovizza village centre, beside Trattoria Al Tiglio - Pri Lipi, Via Bonetti/Basovizza, 34016 Trieste

verified_sources: https://www.masaf.gov.it/flex/cm/pages/ServeBLOB.php/L/IT/IDPagina/11260 (MASAF national monumental-tree register, sheet 69/L424/TS/06, species given as 'Tiglio selvatico'/Tilia cordata, girth 241cm, height 11m)

https://ilregistrodeglialberi.it/16628-tiglio-di-brasovizza-tiglio-trieste-ts-friuli-venezia-giulia (RAMI citizen register, same AMI code 69/L424/TS/06, but recorded species only as 'Tilia sp.' and a conflicting circumference of approx 3.30 m measured 20/08/2024, health 'Buona', field note 'esemplare integro caratterizzato da una forma inconsueta' [a sound specimen with an unusual shape])

https://domenicale.diocesi.trieste.it/2024/10/26/basovizza-la-solidarieta-allombra-del-tiglio/ (Trieste diocese's parish newsletter, describes 'un tiglio secolare' (a centuries-old lime) shading the village square, and the trattoria that sits beneath it)
http://www.basovizza87.it/basovizza/territorio/ (local history page: the trattoria beside the tree dates to the mid-18th century, originally a postal station on the Trieste-Vienna road)
trees.access: Free, stands in the open village square/roadside next to a public trattoria; always visible from the street, no gate reported
trees.transport: Bus 51 from Trieste Centrale (the same line that serves the Foiba di Basovizza memorial), about 20-25 minutes
trees.story:
The inn beside it is named after it, in two languages. Trattoria Al Tiglio, Pri Lipi, which is Italian and Slovene for the same thing: at the lime tree. Basovizza is a Carso village above Trieste that has spoken both for a long time, and the building was a post station on the road from Trieste to Vienna in the middle of the eighteenth century, where travellers changed horses.

How old the lime is, nobody has written down. The parish newsletter calls it secolare, centuries-old, which is the word a village uses about a tree it has always had, and no survey has done better than that. The measurements are no tidier. The national monumental register lists it at 2.41 metres round and 11 metres tall; a field visit in August 2024 put the girth at about 3.30 metres. That gap is too wide to be carelessness with a tape, and the likeliest explanation is the trunk itself, which the same 2024 survey describes as sound but unusually shaped. Somebody put the tape somewhere else.

The good news from that visit is the health rating: good, as of August 2024. It is a small-leaved lime, which means that for a fortnight around midsummer the tree announces itself before you have seen it, and the tables underneath are the obvious place to be while it does.

If you have measured this trunk, tell us where you put the tape.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the shape, which the surveyors call unusual, and by the trattoria beneath it, Al Tiglio, Pri Lipi, named after the tree. It stands in the open in the middle of Basovizza village, 11 metres tall beside the road.

best_time.label: late June into July, when the lime flowers and the scent reaches the road before the tree does

trees.name: The Downy Oak of the University Campus

location.address: Via Licio Giorgieri, Giardini dell'Universita degli Studi di Trieste, 34127 Trieste

verified_sources: https://ilregistrodeglialberi.it/3845-roverella-trieste-ts-friuli-venezia-giulia (RAMI citizen tree register, independent field measurement 14/10/2021, record last updated per site)
trees.access: Free, on the grounds of the University of Trieste's engineering campus (Via Licio Giorgieri). The campus streets and gardens are open, unfenced public ground; no gate or ticket
trees.transport: About 20 min by bus from Piazza Oberdan toward San Giovanni, then a short walk into the campus
trees.story:
Of the forty-eight trees Trieste protects as monumental, one belongs to a university. Il Piccolo's survey of the list noted it in a single line, that the University of Trieste also owns a century-old oak, and that is still more or less all anybody has written about it. The tree is a downy oak, the native oak of the karst plateau that rises behind the city, and it stands in the grounds of the engineering campus off Via Licio Giorgieri in San Giovanni, on university land rather than in a public park.

It is bigger than the setting suggests. Italy's citizen tree register sent someone with a tape in October 2021, who measured the trunk at 3.15 metres round and the crown at fifteen metres tall, at exactly the point where the national and regional registers place it. For a species that usually grows as a scrubby, twisted tree on thin limestone soil, that is a serious girth.

How old it is, nobody has pinned down. "Secolare" is the only word on record, meaning over a century, and it is kept that loose here because the source keeps it that loose. If you know when it was planted, or what stood on this hillside before the campus, tell us.

This is working university ground, not a park: the campus streets are open and unfenced, so walk in, and treat it as the university's tree rather than a city garden's.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, 3.15 metres round on a fifteen-metre oak, the only oak on the university grounds that any register names. It stands on the engineering campus off Via Licio Giorgieri.
trees.verify_notes: Height 15.0 m from the italy-masaf register, matched on our own pin (0 m away).

trees.name: The Second Redwood of Miramare

location.address: Parco del Castello di Miramare, Viale Miramare, 34151 Trieste

verified_sources: https://ilregistrodeglialberi.it/3859-sequoia-sempreverde-trieste-ts-friuli-venezia-giulia (RAMI citizen tree register, independent field measurement 14/10/2021, record last updated per site)
trees.access: Free, the park is open daily. Only the castle charges admission
trees.transport: Bus 6 from Piazza Oberdan to Grignano, about 25 min, then a short walk into the park
trees.story:
Miramare has two protected coast redwoods, and this is the one that loses the argument. It measures 4.01 metres round and twenty-seven metres tall; its neighbour sixty-odd metres to the northeast, the park's headline redwood, is 4.25 metres round and thirty metres tall. Both were measured again in October 2021 by Italy's citizen tree register, which found this trunk at exactly the figure the national register gives.

They are here because of one experiment. When Archduke Maximilian of Habsburg began the park in the spring of 1856 on a bare limestone headland, he wanted to see which foreign trees would take to the Adriatic, and within its first decade the planting included conifers from the fog belt of northern California. Nobody dated this trunk individually, so its age of roughly 170 years is an inference from that campaign rather than a measurement, and it may be a little younger.

What it has outlived is the man. Maximilian left Miramare to become Emperor of Mexico and was shot there in 1867, while redwoods that can live for two thousand years were barely taller than the castle's gardeners.

Stand between the two redwoods and compare the bark: soft, fibrous and red-brown on both, but this is the slimmer trunk and the lower crown.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the soft, fibrous bark of the smaller of Miramare's two redwoods, 4.01 metres round and 27 metres tall. It stands about four metres from the park's protected holm oak.
trees.verify_notes: Height 27.0 m from the italy-masaf register, matched on our own pin (0 m away).

trees.name: The Second Aleppo Pine of Miramare

location.address: Parco del Castello di Miramare, Viale Miramare, 34151 Trieste

verified_sources: https://ilregistrodeglialberi.it/3854-pino-daleppo-trieste-ts-friuli-venezia-giulia (RAMI citizen tree register, independent field measurement 14/10/2021, record last updated per site)
trees.access: Free, the park is open daily. Only the castle charges admission
trees.transport: Bus 6 from Piazza Oberdan to Grignano, about 25 min, then a short walk into the park
trees.story:
The biggest of Miramare's six protected Aleppo pines is also the one nobody has put a date on. It measures 3.68 metres round the trunk and twenty-five metres tall, figures the national register gives and Italy's citizen tree register confirmed with its own tape in October 2021. The only pine of the six with a recorded age is a smaller one, 3.10 metres round, which that citizen register calculated at about 130 years. So the largest pine in the grove is dated here by its sibling and by the park itself: planted some time after the spring of 1856, when Archduke Maximilian began laying out Miramare on a bare limestone point, which puts it somewhere between about 115 and 170 years.

Aleppo pine is the Mediterranean's own survival specialist, named after the Syrian city and built for heat, salt wind and almost no soil, which is roughly what Maximilian's gardeners had to offer before they carted earth onto the rock. It has done well on it. The six stand within a few hundred metres of each other and a stranger would struggle to rank them by eye.

This one sits about fifteen metres from the second largest, and between them they make the grove's heaviest pair. Look for the thickest trunk and the tallest crown in that corner of the park.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the thickest trunk of Miramare's six protected Aleppo pines, 3.68 metres round under a 25-metre crown. It stands about fifteen metres east of a second pine, 3.34 metres round and noticeably lower.
trees.verify_notes: Height 25.0 m from the italy-masaf register, matched on our own pin (0 m away).

trees.story:
Fifteen metres from the largest Aleppo pine at Miramare stands the second largest, and the gap between them is 34 centimetres of girth and five metres of height. This one measures 3.34 metres round and twenty metres tall. Those are the national register's figures, and Italy's citizen tree register found the same trunk at the same point in October 2021, which is as close to certainty as a measurement of a living tree gets.

It belongs to a protected group of six pines in the park, and the group is the point. Archduke Maximilian of Habsburg started Miramare in 1856 as a test of what would grow on a bare limestone promontory above the Adriatic, and a pine built for drought, salt wind and thin soil was the obvious answer to the question he was asking. None of the six is dated individually except a smaller sibling put at about 130 years, so this one is placed somewhere between roughly 115 and 170 years by that sibling and by the park's own start date. Maximilian never saw it grown: he left for Mexico and was shot there in 1867.

If you want to stand between the two heaviest pines in the grove, this is the western half of the pair.

The smallest tree in Miramare's protected pine grove is barely a third of the height of the park's redwoods. It measures 2.13 metres round the trunk and ten metres tall, well below its five siblings, which run from 3.05 to 3.68 metres round and up to twenty-five metres high. It is protected because the grove is. The six Aleppo pines at Miramare are listed as one designated group, and a group listing takes the modest members with the grand ones, which is how a ten-metre pine ends up on the same national register as the largest plane in Trieste. That is not a mistake. A grove planted together reads as a grove, and this is the tree that shows how much the others have grown.

When it went in is unknown. The park itself dates from 1856, when Archduke Maximilian of Habsburg began turning a bare limestone point into a garden, and the grove's one dated pine is put at about 130 years; a smaller trunk does not have to mean a younger tree, so this one gets the same broad span, somewhere between about 115 and 170 years.
